INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND
The objective of this project is to maintain and improve previous performance while
adapting to increased payload and runtime requirements. To achieve this, the new design
incorporates a newly designed 3-Blade propeller, an improved drivetrain configuration, and an
enhanced thermal management system, while refining existing subsystems. Simulation tools
including SolidWorks (2025) for 3D design, ANSYS Workbench (2025R2) for computational
fluid dynamics, and Autodesk Fusion 360 (2026) for modeling are used to evaluate performance
prior to physical prototyping. Proven components from the previous vessel, such as the V-hull and
steering system, are retained, but increased power demands require reevaluation of energy storage
and system reliability.
Electric propulsion in marine applications has evolved significantly since its introduction
in 1839 with early battery-powered boats. While initially favored for quiet operation, electric
vessels were largely replaced by combustion engines due to limited battery technology. Renewed
interest emerged in the late 20th century, with major advancements following the development of
lithium-ion batteries. Modern electric boats now utilize high-voltage systems, efficient motors, and
advanced thermal management to achieve competitive performance. Despite challenges such as
range and infrastructure, electric propulsion continues to expand due to its efficiency, reduced
emissions, and low acoustic signature, which is especially valuable in naval applications.
Overall, the design integrates established marine engineering principles with modern
electric propulsion advancements. By combining simulation-driven design, proven components,
and innovative technologies, the project aims to deliver a vessel optimized for efficiency,
endurance, and reliability within competition constraints.

OVERVIEW OF BUILD AND FABRICATION OF PROCESSES
Design Decisions
Hull
The team initially planned to work with Crevalle Boatworks (Wildwood, Florida), who
offered their scaled-down V-Hull design, the Crevalle 33 CTF, shown in Figure 1. This hull
measured 82 inches in length, 14 inches in beam, and 7.5 inches in hull depth, with ample capacity
for the 60 lbs payload and onboard components. This design included collaboration with Design
Concepts Marine Concepts (Sarasota, Florida) to produce a mold, followed by collaboration with
Vectorply Corporation (Phenix City, Alabama) to manufacture the fiberglass hull.

Figure 1: Crevalle 33 CTF 1/5 Scaled Hull
Delays in mold production extended beyond the allotted timeline, leading to the
abandonment of this design. As a contingency, a premanufactured hull was purchased. The
selected hull, shown in Figure 2, measures 85 inches in length, 18 inches in beam, and 12 inches
in hull depth

Figure 2: Bonzi Sports 84” Classic Hull

Drivetrain
The drivetrain assessment initially evaluated Single and Dual-Propeller configurations,
each with distinct advantages and limitations. A higher-performance single-motor with one shaft
and propeller was chosen to combine the power of the dual system with the stability and space
efficiency of a single configuration (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Single Drivetrain CAD Model
For this configuration the Tenshock Evo 2880 an 8-pole brushless motor engineered to
produce a maximum power of 16,500 Watts, a rotational speed up to 45,000 rpms, and 2.1 Nm of
torque was chosen. This motor features a 10 mm shaft, dictating the minimum diameter of flexible
drive shaft [1]. To sustain increased power demands and mitigate overheating, the SEAKING
300A HV V4 ESC, was selected for its 300A current rating, integrated inner water-cooling
channels, waterproof rating (IP67), three phase compatibility, and Bluetooth function [2].
Due to size and weight constraint, the previous battery was replaced with a MaxAmps
Lithium Batteries (Airway Heights, Washington). Based on the maximum motor amperage of 330
amps and rotational speed of 45,000 RPM, 33,000 RPM were selected as the operational rotational
speed. To meet this, the motor requires a continuous amperage draw of 235 A, and, for an
approximate runtime of 10 minutes at maximum settings, the calculation for capacity (C) using
current (I) and time in hours (H) is shown in (4-1), providing an estimate of required capacity while
omitting reduced speeds for turning/starting or amperage spikes.

To complement computational results, experimental validation was conducted using
propellers printed with Siraya Tech Sculpt-High Temperature Resistant Resin in a testing setup to
compare the performance of the designed and previously used brass propellers. The testing setup
was constructed from a previous hull, rope, and a mechanical force gauge, shown in Figure 14.

Figure 14: Propeller Testing Setup
Four propellers, a prior 3-Blade brass propeller, a prior 4-Blade brass propeller, the
designed toroidal propeller, and the designed 3-Blade propeller, were tested twice each for
consistency, with results summarized in Table 1. The findings confirmed the simulation trends,
showing the toroidal propeller produced significantly lower thrust than the 3-Blade, leading to the
selection of the designed 3-Blade propeller for its superior performance in both simulation and
experimental testing.

With these improvements, and the thermal monitoring system, the electronics should be closer to
their ideal operating temperatures.
Electronics
The electronics system manages communication, telemetry, sensors, and auxiliary
functions while staying isolated from the propulsion battery for stable, long-range operation.
Communications utilize the Boxer Max (M2) radio controller [9] with a long-range
receiver module [10], and operator-side signal booster [11], enabling stable control from beyond
one mile. Antennas are positioned away from the ESC and motor phase wiring to reduce any
electromagnetic interference. Telemetry and sensing are handled by the Arduino Nano ESP32 [12]
microcontroller, selected for its built-in wireless Wi-Fi and Bluetooth functions, and number of
channels. It processes temperature readings from three K-type thermocouples [13] connected
through MAX6675 amplifiers, monitoring multiple points on the ESC’s surface, addressing prior
ESC thermal issues.
All auxiliary electrical components which are the Arduino Nano ESP32, thermocouples,
ESC cooling pump, motor cooling pump, and bilge pump, are powered by the auxiliary battery
from MaxAmps (Spokane, Washington, USA) rated at 10.8 V and 15 Amp-hours [14]. The pumps
draw approximately 0.3 A each, resulting in 0.9 A total, while the Arduino draws 0.2 A and the
thermocouples draw approximately 0.05 A combined, giving a total auxiliary system draw of
approximately 1.25 A. Based on this load, the auxiliary system is capable of operating for
approximately 12 hours on a full charge. The complete electronics architecture is shown in Figure
17.

12

pages.text:
RISK
The design and operation of an uncrewed electric propulsion vessel introduce several risks
that must be mitigated to ensure safety, reliability, and competitive performance. These risks span
electrical, thermal, mechanical, manufacturing, and environmental domains and were addressed
during the design and build process, with additional controls implemented for race conditions.
A primary risk is the high-current electrical system, with operating currents exceeding 200
A and peaks approaching 330 A. This creates potential for overheating, component failure, and
short circuits, as observed in the previous design with ESC failure. To mitigate this, all major

RISK

       The design and operation of an uncrewed electric propulsion vessel introduce several risks

that must be mitigated to ensure safety, reliability, and competitive performance. These risks span

electrical, thermal, mechanical, manufacturing, and environmental domains and were addressed

during the design and build process, with additional controls implemented for race conditions.

       A primary risk is the high-current electrical system, with operating currents exceeding 200

A and peaks approaching 330 A. This creates potential for overheating, component failure, and

short circuits, as observed in the previous design with ESC failure. To mitigate this, all major

components were selected with appropriate safety margins, including a 300A ESC, 400A fuse, and

400A disconnect switch. Wiring is properly sized and insulated for high-current applications, and

acceptable factors of safety. The hull is manufactured using a controlled fiberglass layup over a
CNC mold to ensure consistent geometry and structural integrity. Prior to race operation, all

Manufacturing risks, particularly for the toroidal propeller, include defects such as porosity
or weak bonding when using additive manufacturing. To reduce this risk, additive methods are
limited to prototyping, while final components are expected to be produced using subtractive
manufacturing methods to ensure uniform material properties. All critical components are
inspected before integration.
Water intrusion presents a significant environmental risk, as it can damage electronics and
disrupt system functionality. This is mitigated through sealed enclosures, gasketed hatches, and
marine-grade sealing materials, with a bilge pump included as a secondary safeguard. Leak checks
will be performed prior to launch to verify system integrity.
Communication loss is another key risk, especially for long-range operations. This is
mitigated through a long-range receiver, and signal booster designed to reduce electromagnetic
interference. System checks will verify signal strength before operation.
Risks are mitigated through conservative design practices, appropriate component
selection, thorough testing, and real-time monitoring, ensuring safe and reliable operation under
competition conditions.

pages.text:
CONCLUSION
The finalized vessel design integrates a V-hull, high-power single-motor drivetrain, 3Blade propeller, and thermal management system to address key hydrodynamic, structural, and
operational challenges identified during earlier design phases. The V-hull provides sufficient
internal volume for component integration and payload while maintaining favorable planing
characteristics, low resistance, and directional stability.
The propulsion system consists of a high-torque brushless motor coupled to a single
flexible shaft and optimized 3-Blade propeller with an adjustable trim system. Computational fluid
dynamics analysis using a Reynolds Stress turbulent model, along with experimental thrust testing,
demonstrated that the selected propeller outperforms both prior and toroidal designs at high
rotational speeds. It produces greater thrust, improved flow consistency, and higher overall
efficiency, validating its selection for competition.
Thermal management is achieved through a water-cooling system designed for high-load
operation, with an estimated flow rate of approximately 0.98 GPM. Dual cooling lines and realtime temperature monitoring using thermocouples and an Arduino ESP32 ensure components
remain within safe operating limits.
Structural integrity and durability are addressed through reinforced mounting, sealed
enclosures, improved hatch design, and active bilge management to mitigate vibration and water
ingress. Manufacturing approaches prioritize precision and reliability, transitioning from rapid
prototyping to machined components for critical parts.
Overall, the design represents a balanced integration of hydrodynamic efficiency, thermal
stability, and electrical robustness. Supported by simulation and testing, the vessel meets
performance requirements while maintaining safety and provides a strong foundation for future
optimization of electric marine propulsion systems.
